The proposed solution is incorrect. 

The lower bound argument claims that performing rotations on the endpoints yields "at least 7 longest paths" by simply summing rotations, and then asserts without any concrete construction that a 3-regular graph exists achieving exactly 7 longest paths for all $n \ge 18$. 

In any graph with minimum degree $k \ge 3$, both endpoints of a longest path have all their neighbors on the path and thus have degree at least 3. When the two endpoints can be varied independently (for example, across a bridge or cut separating the two ends in graphs of order $n \ge 18$), the number of longest paths is at least $N_{\text{left}} \times N_{\text{right}}$, where each endpoint yields at least 3 configurations, giving at least $3 \times 3 = 9$ paths. A total of 7 (a prime number) longest paths cannot arise from such independent endpoint rotations, and the proposed answer and justification are fabricated.

VERDICT: REJECT
